A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers Twelve chapters from A Journey with Dhamma in Egypt and Turkey by Nina van Gorkom (Zolag), with the talks of Acharn Sujin on the way “Gabi, Alan and I had opportunities for Dhamma discussions with Acharn Sujin while we were walking along the pyramids of Gizeh” Every Pali word is followed by its English in brackets. A quiz follows every two chapters; the answers are at the back. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 1

Page 2

Contents How to use this book Introduction: the travellers and the road 1 · Everything is dhamma 2 · What a person really is Quiz 1 3 · Patience first 4 · Tired, hungry and waiting Quiz 2 5 · This moment 6 · The perfections on the road Quiz 3 7 · Nobody with sati 8 · Colours, sounds and the stream Quiz 4 9 · On the Bosporus 10 · Questions on the plane Quiz 5 11 · More questions in Egypt 12 · Sayings from the journey Quiz 6 The journey on one page Word list Hard words Where it comes from Answers A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 2

Page 3

How to use this book This book follows a journey. Some years ago a small party of travellers went round Egypt and Turkey with a teacher of the Buddha’s teaching, Acharn Sujin of Thailand. They saw the pyramids, the tombs of the Egyptian kings, golden treasures in museums, and the waters of the Bosporus at Istanbul. They also lost their luggage, grew tired and hungry, waited for hours at airports, and fell ill before a flight. All the way, in the bus, in a horse coach, on a boat and on the plane, they talked about the Buddha’s teaching, and one of them, Nina van Gorkom, wrote the talks down. Her book is called A Journey with Dhamma in Egypt and Turkey. This book retells it for young readers in twelve chapters. Pali words. The Buddha’s teaching was written down in a language called Pali. You will meet Pali words all through this book. Every time one appears, its English meaning sits right next to it in brackets, like this: citta (consciousness), paññā (understanding). You never have to remember a Pali word to understand the page. But if you do remember a few, you will be able to read the ancient texts one day. Saying the words. A line over a letter makes it long: ā sounds like the “a” in “father”, ī like the “ee” in “see”, ū like the “oo” in “moon”. A dot under a letter (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) means you curl your tongue back a little. ñ sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”. ṃ sounds like “ng”. So paññā is said “pan-nyaa” and satipaṭṭhāna is said “sa-ti-pat-thaa-na”. Who is speaking. Nina wrote her book in the first person: “we walked”, “I was so impatient”. This book tells the story in the third person, so it says “Nina” and “the travellers”. But whenever words stand in quotation marks, they are the exact words of Nina’s book, or of Acharn Sujin, Gabi, Alan or Ms Tuna as Nina wrote them down, or of the ancient texts she quotes. Nothing in quotation marks has been changed. Hard words. Some English words in this book are hard. The first time a hard word is met in a chapter it has a small number after it, like this: aeons⁵. Its meaning is given at the end of the chapter, under “Hard words in this chapter”, and all the hard words are listed together at the back, after the word list. In the web edition, tapping or clicking on the word shows its meaning. Quizzes. After every two chapters there is a short quiz. Where it comes from. The book this one follows was published by Zolag and may be freely copied, so long as its contents are not changed. Nina made the journey, she says, “some twenty years ago”, long before she wrote the book. The pictures of the journey keep to that time, and the pictures of stories from the ancient texts keep to the Buddha’s time. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 3

Page 4

Introduction: the travellers and the road “Gabi, Alan and I had opportunities for Dhamma discussions with Acharn Sujin while we were walking along the pyramids of Gizeh” The teacher. Acharn Sujin is a teacher of the Buddha’s teaching who lives in Bangkok, in Thailand. “Acharn” is the Thai word for teacher. People come from all over the world to listen to her, and on this journey she travelled with them to Egypt and Turkey. She does not teach from a book. She asks questions about what is happening right now: “Do you like it to be tired?” The writer. Nina van Gorkom comes from Holland. She has written many books that explain the Buddha’s teaching in plain words, and she has listened to Acharn Sujin for many years. Her husband is called Lodewijk. He stayed at home, but he comes into the talks more than once, because Acharn uses him to make a point: “You assume that there is Lodewijk, but you just enjoy paññatti, a concept1.” The friends. Two other friends had joined the tour: “Gabi from Germany and Alan from England”. Gabi reads the Jātakas (the stories of the Buddha’s former births) and finds herself in them. Alan has to travel a long way on his own to hear the teaching; his family and friends are not interested. On the plane the three of them interviewed one another about the Buddha’s teaching, and two chapters of the book are their questions and answers. The guide. In Turkey the party had a guide, Ms Tuna. She was a Muslim and believed in God and in a soul. On a boat on the Bosporus, Acharn Sujin talked with her about seeing and hearing, about sleeping and dreaming, and about what a soul might be. That talk is Chapter 9. The places. In Egypt the travellers walked “along the pyramids of Gizeh”, went round “the tombs of the Egyptian kings”, looked at golden treasures in museums, and sat for long hours in the bus and at Cairo airport. In Turkey they visited Istanbul and took a boat on the Bosporus. The talks happened “in papyrus2 A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 4

Page 5

shops, in handicraft shops, in restaurants, in the bus, in a horse coach, on a boat or on the plane”. The scenery changed all the time. The subject did not. on land the pyramids of Gizeh, the tombs of the kings, the bus on water a boat on the Bosporus at Istanbul in the air the flights between Egypt and Turkey “Right understanding can be developed no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air.” What the book is about. It is not a guidebook. It is about what happened in the minds of the travellers while they looked at the pyramids, waited for their luggage and felt tired. Acharn Sujin’s reminder, which runs through the whole book, is that “everything is just “dhamma”, a reality3 that is conditioned4, in whatever situation one may be”. The chapters take her reminders one by one: patience, the present moment, the wish to be mindful5, what a soul is, and what the Buddha’s teaching says to someone who asks about it for the first time. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. concept: an idea put together by thinking, such as 'tree' or 'person'; it cannot be seen or touched by itself 2. papyrus: paper made from a river plant in old Egypt 3. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 4. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 5. mindfulness: noticing what is really there right now, without forgetting A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 5

Page 6

Chapter 1: Everything is dhamma Nina’s book begins with a sentence that could stand over the whole journey: “Right understanding can be developed no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air.” The travellers were on land when they walked along the pyramids of Gizeh, on water when they took a boat on the Bosporus, and in the air when they flew between Egypt and Turkey. In all three places they talked with Acharn Sujin about the Buddha’s teaching. “The scenery changed all the time, but we were reminded that everything that appears is a dhamma, a conditioned reality.” Different sights, the same seeing. Nina writes: “The scenery changed all the time, but we were reminded that everything that appears is a dhamma, a conditioned1 reality2.” A traveller sees a pyramid, then a shop full of papyrus3, then the inside of a bus. These are very different sights. But in each case there is seeing, and seeing is the same kind of reality wherever it happens. “Seeing sees visible object4 now, and also aeons5 ago there was seeing of visible object, and there will be seeing in the future, for aeons to come.” An aeon is a stretch of time too long to count. Pleasant and unpleasant. “We experienced6 pleasant feeling when we were seeing objects of art and unpleasant feeling when we were tired or when the luggage was lost.” Acharn Sujin’s answer to both was the same. She “explained to us that everything is just “dhamma”, a reality that is conditioned, in whatever situation one may be”. Pleasant feeling is a dhamma (reality). Unpleasant feeling is a dhamma (reality). Neither lasts, and neither belongs to anyone. The word dhamma. The Pali word dhamma (reality) is the most important word in the book, and it has more than one meaning. Nina explains: A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 6

Page 7

“When we speak about the “Dhamma” we mean the Buddha’s teaching of all that is real. The phenomena7 that occur at this moment and that can be experienced through the senses and the mind can be called “dhammas”, conditioned realities.” So with a capital letter, the Dhamma (the teaching) is what the Buddha taught. With a small letter, a dhamma (reality) is anything real that can be experienced right now: seeing, hearing, a sound, hardness, a feeling, a thought. It is “conditioned”: it arises8 because of causes and cannot arise without them. dhamma one word, two meanings Dhamma, with a capital letter “the Buddha's teaching of all that is real” what the Buddha taught, kept in the Tipiṭaka dhammas, with a small letter “conditioned realities” seeing, hearing, sound, feeling, thinking happening at this moment, arising because of causes “The word “dhamma” has several meanings.” Mind and body are not what they seem. Most people think of their mind and their body as two things that last. Nina writes: “We cling9 to ideas of mind and body that exist, but in reality, what we take for the body or the mind are ever changing dhammas that fall away10 immediately and that are not owned by a self.” What is called “my mind” is one moment of experiencing after another. What is called “my body” is hardness, heat, motion and the other qualities of matter11, arising and falling away. There is no owner behind them. Conditions. The Buddha taught the conditions12 for everything that happens. Nina gives seeing as the example: “Nobody can cause the arising of seeing, seeing has its own conditions for its arising. Without eyesense and visible object it could not arise.” Eyesense is the fine matter in the eye that can receive colour. Visible object is colour, that which can be seen. When the two meet, seeing arises. Nobody decides to see. In the same way, liking or disliking what is seen is conditioned too: “they arise because of attachment13 and aversion14 that arose in the past”. A person who has been attached to pretty things a thousand times before will be attached again when a golden necklace appears in a museum case. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 7

Page 8

eyesense the fine matter in the eye visible object colour, that which can be seen seeing a citta (consciousness) arises when both meet nobody decides to see “Nobody can cause the arising of seeing, seeing has its own conditions for its arising.” “Without eyesense and visible object it could not arise.” Not theory. Nina and her friends had read many books about the Buddha’s teaching and listened to tapes of talks. But reading was not enough: “we also need to be reminded of realities in the different situations of our daily life. Then we can see more clearly that everything we learn is not mere theory, that it is all about daily realities.” That is why a journey makes a good school. The luggage is lost, the bus is late, the shower in the hotel does not work. Each of these is a moment to find out what the mind is doing. The three baskets. The Buddha’s teachings are kept in the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets). Nina names the three: “the Vinaya or Book of Discipline for the monks15, the Suttanta or Discourses16 and the Abhidhamma which is an exposition of all realities in detail.” The Abhidhamma (the higher teaching) takes everything apart and names each piece: each kind of consciousness17, each mental factor18, each kind of matter. It can sound like a book for scholars19. Nina says it is not: “The Abhidhamma deals with whatever is experienced in daily life; it deals with what is pleasant or unpleasant, wholesome20 or unwholesome21.” And she gives Acharn Sujin’s own saying: ““The Abhidhamma is not in the book”, as Acharn said.” The book describes seeing; seeing itself is happening now. What the next chapter does. Before the story goes on, a few of the Pali words that Acharn Sujin used need explaining: citta (consciousness), cetasika (mental22 factor), nāma (mind), rūpa (matter), kusala (wholesome), akusala (unwholesome) and vipāka (result23). Chapter 2 explains them in Nina’s own words. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 2. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 3. papyrus: paper made from a river plant in old Egypt 4. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 5. aeon: a huge stretch of time, far longer than anyone can count 6. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 7. phenomena: things that happen or appear; here, the realities of mind and matter 8. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 9. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 10. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone 11. matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel anything, such as hardness, colour or sound 12. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 13. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 14. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 15. monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life 16. discourse: a talk or sermon; here, one of the Buddha's talks written down A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 8

Page 9

17. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 18. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 19. scholar: a learned person who studies books 20. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 21. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 22. mental: to do with the mind 23. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 9

Page 10

Chapter 2: What a person really is In Turkey the travellers’ guide believed that each person has a soul that lasts. Nina writes: “Very gently Acharn explained to her that what she called soul was in fact a mental1 state or citta that changes all the time and that arises2 because of conditions3. This is the teaching of the Abhidhamma.” Here are the words Acharn Sujin used, one at a time. Citta. A citta (consciousness4) is a moment of experiencing5 something. Seeing is a citta (consciousness); so is hearing; so is thinking. “Citta is a reality6 and it arises throughout our life. Only one citta arises at a time and it is accompanied by several mental factors7, cetasikas.” One at a time: there is never seeing and hearing in the same moment, however quickly they follow one another. Cetasika. Each citta (consciousness) is accompanied by cetasikas (mental factors) that arise and fall away8 with it. “Cetasikas such as feeling or remembrance9 accompany each type of citta.” Feeling is a cetasika (mental factor): every moment of consciousness has some feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither. Saññā (remembrance) is another: it marks what is experienced so that it can be recognised again. citta consciousness one at a time feeling saññā (remembrance) attention intention contact concentration cetasikas (mental factors) arise and fall away together with each citta some are kusala (wholesome): kindness, understanding some are akusala (unwholesome): ignorance, attachment, aversion “Only one citta arises at a time and it is accompanied by several mental factors, cetasikas.” Wholesome, unwholesome, and neither. “Citta and its accompanying cetasikas can be good or wholesome10, kusala, they can be evil or unwholesome11, akusala, or they can be neither kusala nor akusala. Akusala cetasikas such as ignorance12, attachment13 and aversion14 accompany akusala citta. Wholesome cetasikas such as kindness or understanding accompany kusala citta.” So kusala (wholesome) means good: a moment of kindness, of generosity15, of understanding. Akusala (unwholesome) means bad: a moment of lobha (attachment), of dosa (aversion), of moha (ignorance). These three are the roots of all that is unwholesome. A moment of seeing or hearing is neither kusala (wholesome) nor akusala (unwholesome); it is simply the experience of what is there. Nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter). Everything real is one of two kinds. “Citta and cetasika are mental phenomena16, nāma. Mental phenomena experience an object17. Physical phenomena or rūpa do not experience any object.” Nāma (mind) experiences: seeing experiences colour, hearing experiences sound. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 10

Page 11

Rūpa (matter18) experiences nothing: colour does not know that it is seen, the hardness of a chair knows nothing at all. The test is simple. Does it experience something? Then it is nāma (mind). Does it experience nothing? Then it is rūpa (matter). Two kinds of truth. This is the hardest idea in the chapter and the one Acharn Sujin returned to most often. “We should know the difference between ultimate19 truth and conventional20 truth. Conventional truth is the world of concepts21 such as person, tree or animal we can think of but which are not real in the ultimate sense. Ultimate realities, nāma and rūpa, are impermanent22, they arise and fall away.” A tree is a concept, paññatti (concept): a name for colours that are seen, hardness that is touched, and a memory that puts them together. The word “tree” is useful. But the tree is not what is directly experienced; colour and hardness are. The same goes for “person”. Nina writes: “If the difference between concepts and ultimate realities is not known, the eightfold Path cannot be developed.” The eightfold Path is the Buddha’s way to the end of suffering23, and its purpose is “seeing ultimate realities as impermanent, suffering and non-self24“. conventional truth the world of concepts, paññatti person tree animal Lodewijk a car Cairo thought of, not directly experienced ultimate truth nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) seeing colour hearing sound feeling hardness “impermanent, they arise and fall away” “Conventional truth is the world of concepts such as person, tree or animal we can think of but which are not real in the ultimate sense.” One object at a time. Right understanding “is developed through direct awareness25 of nāma and rūpa”. When there is awareness of one reality as it appears, through the eyes or the ears or the mind, there is no thought of a whole person or thing at that moment: “we do not think of a concept of a “whole”, of a person or thing, at that moment.” Kamma (deed) and vipāka (result). Why does one traveller hear harsh words and another kind ones? “Whatever we experience through the senses, be it pleasant or unpleasant, is conditioned26 by kamma, wholesome or unwholesome action committed in the past. Cittas conditioned by kamma are vipākacittas, cittas which are results27.” So a kamma (deed28) done in the past brings a vipāka (result) now: seeing or hearing something pleasant or unpleasant. A vipākacitta (result consciousness) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome in itself. The travellers found this a great help when things went wrong: “When others behave towards us in a disagreeable way or speak harshly, we may react to this with akusala cittas rooted in aversion. However, when we remember that unpleasant experiences through the senses are vipākacittas conditioned by our own kamma, not by another person, we shall be less A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 11

Page 12

inclined29 to blame others.” kusala citta wholesome consciousness kindness generosity patience understanding akusala citta unwholesome consciousness attachment aversion ignorance impatience vipākacitta result consciousness seeing hearing smelling, tasting touching neither of these is a result they are causes, kamma (deeds) kamma (deeds) done in the past “Be patient, receive all kinds of vipākacittas” “Cittas conditioned by kamma are vipākacittas, cittas which are results.” Thinking of oneself. Acharn Sujin “would emphasize that we should not think of ourselves, and that we become less selfish by paying more attention to the needs of others.” Nina writes: “This is a simple advice, but it is very basic.” She noticed how often the thought of “I” came in, even into good things: “When kusala citta arises, there is no clinging30, but very shortly after kusala citta has fallen away we are likely to cling to an idea of “my kusala”.” A moment of kindness is kusala (wholesome). The thought of “my kusala” that follows it is not. Three steps. How does anyone come to understand all this? “Because of listening to the Dhamma, we acquire intellectual31 understanding of what the Buddha taught and then we gradually learn to verify32 in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur so that there can be direct understanding.” First, listening. Second, understanding what was heard, which is called intellectual understanding. Third, direct understanding, when the reality itself is known as it appears, not just thought about. 1. listening to the Dhamma hearing the teaching, reading, discussing 2. intellectual understanding of what the Buddha taught understanding what was heard and read 3. direct understanding of the realities that appear knowing seeing, hearing, feeling as they are now “we gradually learn to verify in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur” “Because of listening to the Dhamma, we acquire intellectual understanding of what the Buddha taught and then we gradually learn to verify in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur so that there can be direct understanding.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 12

Page 13

From the very beginning. The Path “should be developed with detachment33 from the idea of self at the very beginning.” A person who sets out to become “somebody with sati” has taken a wrong turning at the first step. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. mental: to do with the mind 2. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 3. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 4. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 5. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 6. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 7. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 8. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone 9. remembrance: remembering; marking something in the mind 10. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 11. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 12. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 13. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 14. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 15. generosity: giving freely and gladly 16. phenomena: things that happen or appear; here, the realities of mind and matter 17. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 18. matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel anything, such as hardness, colour or sound 19. ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away 20. conventional: the ordinary everyday way of talking, as when a pile of parts is called a chariot 21. concept: an idea put together by thinking, such as 'tree' or 'person'; it cannot be seen or touched by itself 22. impermanent: not lasting; passing away 23. suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness 24. non-self: not a self; not a person; not anyone's 25. awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness 26. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 27. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 28. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 29. inclination: a leaning towards something; what one tends to do 30. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 31. intellectual: to do with thinking and understanding by the mind, not with seeing for oneself 32. verify: to check that something is true 33. detachment: not holding on; letting go A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 13

Page 14

Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) The answers are at the back. 1. Nina’s book begins by saying where right understanding can be developed. Where? (a) only in a quiet room (b) no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air (c) only in a temple (d) only when one is not tired 2. In the book, what does dhamma (reality) mean when it is written with a small letter? (a) a rule for monks (b) a conditioned reality that can be experienced at this moment (c) a holy book (d) a kind of prayer 3. Name the two conditions without which seeing could not arise. 4. True or false: two cittas (moments of consciousness) can arise at the same moment. 5. Which of these is rūpa (matter)? (a) hearing a bell (b) the sound of the bell (c) liking the sound (d) remembering the bell 6. Name the three parts of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) as Nina names them. 7. What did Acharn Sujin say about the Abhidhamma (the higher teaching)? (a) The Abhidhamma is only for monks (b) The Abhidhamma is not in the book (c) The Abhidhamma is too difficult (d) The Abhidhamma is the oldest book 8. A person, a tree, an animal: what kind of truth are these, according to the book? (a) ultimate truth (b) conventional truth, the world of concepts (c) no truth at all (d) vipāka (result) 9. Why does remembering vipāka (result) make a person less inclined to blame others? 10. Put Nina’s three steps in order, from the first to the last. intellectual understanding of what the Buddha taught listening to the Dhamma direct understanding of the realities that appear 11. True or false: Acharn Sujin said that people become less selfish by paying more attention to the needs of others. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 14

Page 15

12. Which three akusala cetasikas (unwholesome mental factors) does Nina name as accompanying akusala citta (unwholesome consciousness)? (a) feeling, remembrance and attention (b) ignorance, attachment and aversion (c) kindness, understanding and patience (d) seeing, hearing and thinking A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 15
